## Simple explanation

BERT is a language model that reads text using context from both directions.
Its pretrained representations can be adapted to tasks such as
classification and question answering.

## Technical explanation

BERT uses a stack of Transformer encoder layers. Its original pretraining
included masked language modeling, where selected tokens are hidden and
predicted from surrounding context, and next-sentence prediction. Unlike a
causal language model, a BERT encoder can attend to tokens on both sides
when constructing contextual representations.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

BERT established a widely used approach to pretraining bidirectional
representations and adapting them to language tasks. It is useful to
understand encoder models when selecting architectures for classification,
ranking, extraction, and other tasks that do not require left-to-right
generation.

## How it works

Text is tokenized into subword units and augmented with position and
segment information. The encoder layers contextualize the tokens through
self-attention. A task-specific head can then use token or pooled
representations to make predictions.

## Practical example

For sentiment classification, a BERT encoder processes the review text and
a classification head maps a sequence representation to sentiment scores.
The model can be fine-tuned using labeled examples.

## Common misconceptions

- BERT is an encoder model, not a standard left-to-right text generator.
- "Bidirectional" describes how context is used by the encoder; it does not
  mean BERT sees future information unavailable in every downstream task.
- Pretraining does not guarantee good performance without suitable
  fine-tuning or evaluation.
